question_text: When operating a motor boat near a person in the water, the maximum speed you must not exceed within 50 metres is:
answer_a: 4 knots
answer_c: 8 knots

question_text: Within 15 metres of a vessel that is underway, what is the maximum speed limit?
answer_a: 4 knots
answer_c: 8 knots

question_text: What is the maximum speed limit within a mooring area or boat haven?
answer_a: 4 knots
answer_c: 8 knots

question_text: Which of the following boating accidents must be reported to authorities?
answer_a: All accidents, no matter how minor.
answer_b: Only accidents involving motor boats or water skiers.
answer_c: Accidents resulting in serious injury or death, or that leave the vessel unseaworthy or unsafe.
answer_d: Only accidents involving property damage over $1,000.

question_text: Which vessels are generally required to be registered?
answer_a: Only vessels fitted with an engine of 5 hp or more.
answer_b: All recreational vessels that are, or can be, fitted with an engine, other than a tender.
answer_c: All recreational vessels over 3.1 metres fitted with an engine.
answer_d: No vessels are required to be registered.

question_text: A dive flag (a white flag with a diagonal blue stripe) seen on the water means:
answer_a: Dangerous cargo is on board — keep well away.
answer_b: A diver is below — keep 50 metres clear, or travel at the slowest possible speed with a good lookout for people in the water.
answer_c: Shallow water ahead — proceed with caution.
answer_d: A vessel is aground — keep clear.

question_text: An RST entitles the holder to skipper:
answer_a: Vessels under 8 metres in length only.
answer_c: All commercial vessels.

question_text: Within 50 metres of a jetty, wharf or the shore, the maximum speed limit is:
answer_a: 8 knots
answer_c: 10 knots

question_text: An RST holder under the age of 16 is restricted to operating a vessel:
answer_a: That is less than 4 metres in length.
answer_c: During daylight hours and at a speed of less than 8 knots.

question_text: What is the maximum blood alcohol limit that applies to the skipper of a recreational vessel in WA?
A marine incident involving serious injury, death, or damage that leaves a vessel unseaworthy must be reported within:
answer_a: 24 hours.
answer_c: 72 hours.

question_text: If you come across another vessel or person in distress on the water, as skipper you are expected to:
answer_a: Offer assistance, within the limits of what you can safely do.
answer_b: Continue on your way unless directly asked for help.
answer_c: Only assist if you are the closest vessel and fully crewed.
answer_d: Radio the coastguard and take no further action yourself.

question_text: A small tender fitted with a motor of 5 hp or less, and no longer than 3.1 metres, is generally:
answer_a: Required to be registered the same as any other vessel.
answer_c: Only exempt if used exclusively at night.
answer_d: Required to display a special exemption sticker.

question_text: Which code flag is used to signal that a diver is below?
answer_a: Code flag A.
answer_c: Code flag O.

question_text: Water skiing behind a recreational vessel requires, at minimum:
answer_a: A skipper only.
answer_c: A skipper, an observer, and a skier who all meet the age and role requirements.
answer_d: Any two people on board, regardless of role.

question_text: While a vessel is underway, passengers should:
answer_a: Stay within the hull of the vessel — not perched on the bow or gunwales.
answer_b: Sit on the bow for a better view, if the water is calm.
answer_c: Stand on the gunwales when taking photos.
answer_d: Sit wherever they like, provided they hold on.

question_text: If you change your name or residential address after obtaining your RST, you must:
answer_a: Do nothing — RST details never need updating.
answer_c: Re-sit the theory assessment.
answer_d: Notify your local marine rescue group only.

question_text: You have right of way and an approaching motor boat doesn't seem to be taking action to prevent a collision. What should you do?
answer_a: Speed up so you can get past in time.
answer_b: Exercise caution and take whatever avoiding action is necessary.
answer_c: Maintain your course and speed because you have right of way.
answer_d: Let off an internationally recognised distress signal.

question_text: What does keeping a good lookout actually involve?
answer_a: Looking straight ahead.
answer_b: Looking forward and to each side.
answer_c: Looking behind you.
answer_d: Using sight, hearing and all other available means.

question_text: You are overtaking another vessel. What must you do?
answer_a: Overtake on the starboard (right) side only.
answer_b: Overtake on the port (left) side only.
answer_c: Keep well clear of the vessel you are overtaking, on either side.

question_text: When travelling upstream in a narrow channel or river, where should you keep your vessel?
answer_a: On the port (left-hand) side.
answer_c: In the middle of the channel.
answer_d: On either side, whichever is safe.

question_text: What sound signal means 'I am operating astern propulsion'?
answer_a: Three short blasts.
answer_c: One short blast.

question_text: Two vessels are approaching each other as shown, one directly ahead and slightly to the right of the other. Which vessel must give way?
answer_a: The vessel with the other boat on its starboard (right) side.
answer_b: The vessel with the other boat on its port (left) side.
answer_c: Neither — they should both hold course until one gives way.

question_text: In restricted visibility such as fog or heavy rain, you should:
answer_a: Speed up to get through the area faster.
answer_b: Switch on navigation lights, slow to a safe speed, and keep an especially good lookout.
answer_c: Switch off your motor and drift until visibility improves.
answer_d: Continue as normal — restricted visibility does not change the rules.

question_text: A vessel that is hampered by the work it is doing, such as dredging or cable laying, generally:
answer_a: Must always give way to power-driven vessels.
answer_b: Has right of way over ordinary traffic.
answer_c: Has no special status under the rules.

question_text: As a general rule between a power-driven vessel and a sailing vessel, which must give way?
answer_a: The sailing vessel.
answer_c: Whichever is travelling faster.

question_text: What does five short blasts on a vessel's horn mean?
answer_a: I am altering course to starboard.
answer_b: I am altering course to port.
answer_c: I am operating astern propulsion.
answer_d: I do not understand your intentions, or you are not taking sufficient action.

question_text: You are on a crossing course with another power-driven vessel on your port (left) side. You believe they may not have seen you. You should:
answer_a: Hold your course and speed, since you have right of way.
answer_b: Alter course to the right, slow down, or both, even though you technically have right of way.
answer_c: Alter course to the left to move away faster.
answer_d: Sound one short blast and take no further action.

question_text: Two power-driven vessels are meeting head-on. What action should both take?
answer_a: Both alter course to the right, passing port-to-port.
answer_b: Both alter course to the left, passing starboard-to-starboard.
answer_c: One should stop; the other proceeds.

question_text: What lights are required on a motor boat under 12 metres in length when underway at night or in reduced visibility?
answer_a: Sidelights and a green masthead light.
answer_c: Red and green sidelights only, with no other light.
answer_d: Red and green sidelights, plus either an all-round white light or a masthead light and stern light.

question_text: On a vessel under 12 metres, what is the minimum distance a masthead light must be visible from?
answer_a: 1 nautical mile.
answer_c: 3 nautical miles.

question_text: On a vessel that carries a masthead light, how high above the gunwale must it be mounted, at minimum?
answer_a: 1 metre.
answer_c: 2 metres.

question_text: What happens to rhodopsin, the molecule in your eyes responsible for night vision, when exposed to a bright white light?
answer_a: It bleaches out, and full night vision can take the better part of an hour to recover.
answer_b: It has no real effect on night vision.
answer_c: It permanently improves night vision.
answer_d: It turns the surrounding area red.

question_text: A sailing vessel over 20 metres with separate sidelights and a stern light may also carry two optional all-round lights near the top of the mast. What colour is the upper light?
answer_a: White.
answer_c: Green.

question_text: Between sunset and sunrise, the general open-water speed limit on the Swan and Canning rivers reduces to:
answer_a: 6 knots.
answer_c: 10 knots.

question_text: What lights must a vessel over 50 metres in length show while at anchor?
answer_a: A single all-round white light.
answer_b: Two all-round white lights, with the forward light higher than the aft light.
answer_c: Two all-round white lights, with the aft light higher than the forward light.

question_text: What is the minimum lighting requirement for a motor boat under 7 metres travelling at 7 knots or less, underway at night?
answer_a: Sidelights only, with no other light required.
answer_b: A visible all-round white light, and sidelights if practicable.
answer_c: A masthead light and stern light only.
answer_d: No lights are required at that speed.

question_text: On a vessel under 12 metres, the masthead and stern lights may be combined into:
answer_a: A single all-round white light.
answer_c: Two separate green lights.
answer_d: They can never be combined, regardless of vessel size.

question_text: A sailing vessel that is motoring, rather than sailing, must show:
answer_a: No lights at all, since it is a sailing vessel.
answer_c: The same lights as a motor boat of its size.

question_text: Why should you use red light rather than white light at the helm or chart table at night?
answer_a: Red light uses less battery power.
answer_b: White light bleaches out night vision, which can take up to an hour to fully recover.
answer_c: Red light is required by law after sunset.
answer_d: There is no real difference between red and white light at night.

question_text: What kind of navigation mark has two black spheres, one above the other, as its topmark?
answer_a: A port lateral mark.
answer_c: A safe water mark.

question_text: A cardinal mark has lost its topmark. The colour bands on the pole, from top to bottom, are black, yellow, black. What type of cardinal mark is it?
answer_a: West cardinal.
answer_c: North cardinal.

question_text: Which colours are used for lateral mark lights?
answer_a: Red and green only — the only marks that use these colours.
answer_c: Yellow only.

question_text: Which light rhythm is specifically kept away from ordinary lateral marks, to avoid confusion?
answer_a: Flashing.
answer_c: Group Flashing.

question_text: If lit, a Safe Water Mark will NOT normally show which of the following rhythms?
answer_a: Isophase.
answer_c: Composite Group Flashing.

question_text: What colour light does a Special Mark show, if lit?
answer_a: White.
answer_c: Red.

question_text: Which of the following is NOT a typical use of a Special Mark?
answer_a: Marking a traffic separation zone.
answer_c: Marking an aquaculture lease.
answer_d: Marking the port side of a channel.

question_text: A light shows a continuous flashing pattern at a rate of 50 to 60 flashes per minute. What type of light is this?
answer_a: Isophase.
answer_c: Very Quick Flashing.

question_text: When using a pair of leads to steer a safe course, if the marks are lit, what colour must the lights be?
answer_a: Always red.
answer_c: Always green.
answer_d: Any colour — the chart will show what to expect.

question_text: Entering a harbour, on which side should you keep a red, can-shaped port lateral mark?
answer_a: On your port (left) side.
answer_c: It does not matter which side.
answer_d: Directly ahead, in the centre of the channel.

question_text: A North cardinal mark's black topmark cones both point:
answer_a: Up.
answer_c: Away from each other.

question_text: What does an Isolated Danger Mark indicate?
answer_a: Safe water in every direction.
answer_b: A specific hazard, with safe water all around it — pass well clear on any side.
answer_c: The port side of a channel.

question_text: How often should the motor on your vessel be serviced?
answer_a: Before each time you use the vessel.
answer_c: At least once a year.

question_text: Before you go on a boating trip, you should:
answer_a: Test navigation lights.
answer_b: Check bilges are clean and dry.
answer_c: Check steering.

question_text: Why should you replace old fuel after a long period of inactivity?
answer_a: Your vessel won't reach top speed.
answer_b: The oil will settle on the bottom of the tank.
answer_c: The octane level will reduce over time.
answer_d: Water is likely to have built up in it.

question_text: Where should batteries in a vessel be located?
answer_a: In a ventilated container.
answer_c: As low as possible in the bilge.
answer_d: On deck, exposed to the elements.

question_text: If your vessel is fitted with an LP gas system, how often should it be serviced?
answer_a: Before each trip.
answer_c: Monthly.

question_text: If you use your motor hard, how often should the gearbox oil be changed?
answer_a: Every month.
answer_c: Every six months.

question_text: What is the most common cause of electrical system failures on a vessel?
answer_a: Corrosion of terminals and connectors.
answer_c: Using the wrong colour wiring.

question_text: Before starting your motor, a good habit is to do a 'sniff test' to check for:
answer_a: Fuel smell, which could indicate a leak.
answer_c: Salt water residue.

question_text: After every trip, you should flush your engine with:
answer_a: Salt water.
answer_c: Diesel.
answer_d: Nothing — flushing is only needed monthly.

question_text: As part of a monthly maintenance check, you should:
answer_a: Check flares and EVDS are still in date.
answer_c: Look over safety gear for signs of deterioration.

question_text: As part of a yearly maintenance check, you should inspect:
answer_a: Anodes for erosion.
answer_c: The gearbox oil, and replace it.

question_text: Why should you periodically remove the propeller and check the shaft for wrapped fishing line?
answer_a: It has no real effect and is purely cosmetic.
answer_b: Wrapped line can destroy the gearbox seal and let water in, eventually wrecking the gearbox.
answer_c: It only affects top speed, not the gearbox.
answer_d: Fishing line cannot wrap around a propeller shaft.

question_text: Where should safety equipment such as flares, EVDS and lifejackets be stowed on a vessel?
answer_a: In readily accessible positions, protected from the sea and weather.
answer_c: Away from passengers, so they can't accidentally damage them.
answer_d: Anywhere on board — location doesn't matter.

question_text: What safety equipment MUST be carried on a registrable vessel operating in unprotected waters, more than 4 nautical miles from the coast?
answer_a: Two orange and two red hand-held flares, or EVDS.
answer_c: An HF or VHF marine radio.

question_text: Fire extinguishers are recommended to be carried on vessels that:
answer_a: Are propelled by an inboard motor, or have cooking, heating or cooling equipment that uses flame.
answer_b: Are propelled by an outboard motor.
answer_c: Do not carry a fire blanket.
answer_d: Are propelled by an electric motor.

question_text: When anchoring a vessel, you should consider:
answer_a: The length of anchor line you'll need.
answer_c: Whether the vessel might drift.

question_text: How many lifejackets must be carried on board a registrable vessel in unprotected waters?
answer_a: One for each person on board.
answer_c: Six.

question_text: Other than using your radio in a distress situation, what is the most effective way of attracting attention at night?
answer_a: Waving your arms up and down.
answer_b: Letting off an orange smoke flare.
answer_c: Using an EVDS or a red hand-held flare.
answer_d: All of the above are equally effective.

question_text: When should you activate your EPIRB or PLB?
answer_a: As soon as the motor cuts out and won't restart.
answer_b: Only where human life is in grave and imminent danger.
answer_c: Any time you run out of fuel.

question_text: When must an approved marine band radio be carried?
answer_a: On all vessels, on all waters.
answer_b: On all registrable vessels operating beyond 4 nautical miles from shore.
answer_c: On all non-registrable vessels operating beyond 4 nautical miles from shore.
answer_d: On all vessels operating in unprotected waters, regardless of distance.

question_text: What do the words 'Pan Pan' indicate when said at the start of a radio message?
answer_a: A very urgent message follows, concerning the safety of a vessel or person, but it is not a grave and imminent danger.
answer_b: A vessel is in grave and imminent danger.
answer_c: An important navigational warning is about to be announced.

question_text: What standard must an approved lifejacket meet?
answer_a: AS 4758 or ISO 12402.
answer_c: There is no standard — any flotation device is acceptable.

question_text: What is the key difference between a Level 100+ lifejacket and a Level 50/50S lifejacket?
answer_a: Level 100+ jackets provide head and neck support and float the wearer face-up; Level 50/50S do not.
answer_b: Level 50/50S jackets are always more buoyant.
answer_c: There is no practical difference between them.
answer_d: Level 100+ jackets are only for use on PWCs.

question_text: Approximately how long does a red hand-held distress flare burn for?
answer_a: About 45 seconds.
answer_c: About 10 minutes.

question_text: An EPIRB is designed to float and operate for a minimum of:
answer_a: 12 hours.
answer_c: 48 hours.

question_text: A PLB (Personal Locator Beacon) differs from an EPIRB in that it:
answer_a: Must be worn by a person on board and operates for a minimum of 24 hours.
answer_b: Floats free of the vessel and never needs to be worn.
answer_c: Does not need to be registered with AMSA.

question_text: What is the designated international distress and calling channel on a VHF marine radio?
answer_a: Channel 9.
answer_c: Channel 67.

question_text: What is the recommended anchor line 'scope' (length of line relative to water depth) in calm conditions?
answer_a: At least twice the water depth.
answer_b: At least five times the water depth.
answer_c: Exactly the water depth.
answer_d: Scope does not matter in calm conditions.

question_text: As part of your trip plan you should ensure:
answer_a: Your vessel is suitable for the trip.
answer_b: The weather and tides are favourable.
answer_c: All your safety gear and extras are on board, in good shape and within reach.

question_text: How much additional fuel is recommended to carry for a boating trip, over and above what you expect to use?
answer_a: 10% more than you expect to use.
answer_b: 20% more than you expect to use.
answer_c: 50% more than you expect to use.
answer_d: 100% more than you expect to use.

question_text: Which is the most up-to-date source of weather forecasts?
answer_a: The Bureau of Meteorology.
answer_c: Last night's television news.

question_text: Which wind warning indicates the average wind speed is expected to be 25 to 33 knots?
answer_a: Strong wind warning.
answer_c: Storm warning.

question_text: Before undertaking a recreational boating trip, when should you tell relatives, friends or local authorities your travel plans and estimated arrival or return time?
answer_a: Only when bad weather is forecast.
answer_c: On every occasion.

question_text: When loading your vessel with passengers and equipment for a day's outing, you should:
answer_a: Distribute the load evenly in the vessel.
answer_b: Ensure adequate freeboard for the conditions and any unexpected deterioration in weather.
answer_c: Keep passenger numbers within the recommended limit.

question_text: If a vessel fills with water and has basic flotation, it will:
answer_a: Sink straight away.
answer_b: Have enough flotation to prevent the vessel and its maximum load from sinking.
answer_c: Take three hours to sink.

question_text: In the southern hemisphere, a low pressure system rotates in which direction?
answer_a: Clockwise.
answer_c: Always north.

question_text: Which of the following can be a sign of approaching bad weather?
answer_a: A wind shift.
answer_c: Cloud building up.

question_text: How do you work out your vessel's fuel consumption in litres per hour?
answer_a: Divide litres used by hours run on a typical trip.
answer_b: Multiply litres used by hours run.
answer_c: It cannot be estimated — you must ask the manufacturer.
answer_d: Divide the tank capacity by the trip distance.

question_text: Before departing, what crew factors should a skipper consider?
answer_a: Whether anyone is prone to seasickness.
answer_b: Whether anyone has a medical condition the skipper should know about.
answer_c: Whether the trip is appropriate for everyone's age and experience.

question_text: What is 'free surface effect'?
answer_a: Water sloshing around loose inside the hull, which can seriously undermine stability.
answer_b: The natural buoyancy of an empty hull.
answer_c: The drag caused by a fouled propeller.
answer_d: The effect of wind on an anchored vessel.

question_text: A vessel with a long, slow roll that is reluctant to return upright is showing signs of:
answer_a: Being correctly loaded.
answer_b: Instability — weight should be moved lower and load reduced.
answer_c: A simple list, which is not a safety concern.
answer_d: Normal behaviour in any sea state.

question_text: What is 'chart datum'?
answer_a: The average high tide level.
answer_b: Roughly the lowest water level the tide is likely to fall to, from which charted depths are measured.
answer_c: The exact depth at every point on a chart, regardless of tide.
answer_d: A GPS reference point unrelated to tides.

question_text: A sudden, brief increase in wind speed, often with a change in direction, that dies away again is called a:
answer_a: Gale.
answer_c: Gust.

question_text: Your vessel capsizes 4 nautical miles from the mainland shore. In most circumstances, it is best to:
answer_a: Swim away from the vessel.
answer_b: Try swimming to the shore as a group.
answer_c: Send the strongest swimmer to get help.

question_text: Most vessel groundings can be avoided by:
answer_a: Planning your trips using a chart.
answer_b: Knowing what navigation marks look like and mean.
answer_c: Slowing down if you are unsure of a situation.

question_text: You are out in a motor boat in calm weather and the motor cuts out unexpectedly. What should you do first?
answer_a: Fire flares.
answer_c: Drop the anchor and assess your options.

question_text: Fuel vapour will not leave a compartment without assistance because:
answer_a: Fuel vapour is the same weight as air.
answer_b: Fuel vapour is lighter than air.
answer_c: Fuel vapour is heavier than air.

question_text: After a period of being exposed to cold water, the most likely effect on the body will be:
answer_a: Hunger.
answer_c: Dehydration.

question_text: Who is responsible for the safety of everyone on board a recreational vessel?
answer_a: The owner or their representative.
answer_b: The most experienced person on board.
answer_c: Any qualified person.

question_text: Which of the following is a common contributing factor in vessel capsizes?
answer_a: Overloading or poor load distribution.
answer_c: Free surface effect from water sloshing in the hull.

question_text: Before abandoning a sinking vessel, if time allows, you should:
answer_a: Remove excess clothing to swim more easily.
answer_b: Try to send a Mayday call and activate your EPIRB.
answer_c: Empty the fuel tank overboard.
answer_d: Wait until the vessel is fully submerged before acting.

question_text: If your vessel runs aground, what should you check first?
answer_a: Whether your passengers are safe and uninjured.
answer_c: Whether anyone saw it happen.
answer_d: The state of the tide only.

question_text: Which of these is a common cause of fire on a recreational vessel?
answer_a: Overheated galley equipment.
answer_c: Poor refuelling technique.

question_text: If a fire breaks out on your vessel, an early priority is to:
answer_a: Raise the alarm and do a head count.
answer_b: Continue on course and monitor the fire from a distance.
answer_c: Immediately abandon ship regardless of the fire's size.
answer_d: Turn off all radios to avoid distraction.

question_text: If your motor won't start, a basic troubleshooting check should include:
answer_a: The kill switch and fuel supply.
answer_b: Battery connections, spark plugs and fuses.
answer_c: The choke and carburettor air intake.

question_text: What is the key difference between the HELP position and the Huddle position?
answer_a: HELP is used alone; Huddle is used by a group clustering together for warmth.
answer_b: HELP is only for use in warm water; Huddle is for cold water.
answer_c: There is no difference — they are the same technique.
answer_d: Huddle is used alone; HELP is used by a group.
